subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 18! In this unit you will learn how to describe exactly where things are and how they move. Every day you already do this without thinking. When Amina tells Yusuf that the well is 'two streets north, then one street east', she is describing a position and a movement. When Hassan follows a map from Hargeisa to the market, he is using directions. When Khadija folds a paper to make a matching pattern for Eid, she is using a reflection. In this unit you will learn to do all of these things carefully and mathematically.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 4 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Use the eight compass directions (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW) to describe direction and movement.
Use coordinates to describe the position of a point in the first quadrant.
Plot points on a coordinate grid and read the coordinates of a marked point.
Describe a movement on a grid using coordinates and directions.
Reflect 2D shapes across vertical and horizontal mirror lines.
Identify the properties of reflected shapes (same size, same shape, equal distances).
Find the coordinates of a reflected point using a mirror line.
Apply position, direction and movement to solve real-world problems and read simple maps.

concepts.title: The Eight Compass Directions
concepts.explanation:
A compass is a tool that helps us find our way by showing directions. It has four main directions. Picture a map spread out on the table in front of you:

North (N) points toward the top of the map.

East (E) points toward the right of the map.

South (S) points toward the bottom of the map.

West (W) points toward the left of the map.

Between these four main directions lie four more, called the in-between or diagonal directions. Each one is made by joining the names of the two main directions on either side of it:

North-East (NE) lies between North and East (top-right).

South-East (SE) lies between South and East (bottom-right).

South-West (SW) lies between South and West (bottom-left).

North-West (NW) lies between North and West (top-left).

Together these eight directions form a compass rose. Imagine a star with eight arms. If you stand in the middle facing North and turn slowly to your right (clockwise), you pass through NE, then E, then SE, then S, then SW, then W, then NW, and finally back to N. Picture it drawn like this, with North at the top:

N is at the top, S is at the bottom, W is on the left and E is on the right. NW sits in the top-left corner, NE in the top-right, SW in the bottom-left, and SE in the bottom-right.

A useful memory trick for the order going clockwise from the top is 'Never Eat Soggy Weetabix' for North, East, South, West. Once you know those four in order, the in-between directions are easy: each simply combines the two main directions it sits between. Notice we always say the North or South part first – we write NE and SW, never 'EN' or 'WS'.
concepts.example: Directions come in opposite pairs. North is opposite South. East is opposite West. North-East is opposite South-West. North-West is opposite South-East. If Farah walks North-East to reach the masjid, then to walk straight home again she must go in the exact opposite direction, South-West. Knowing opposites helps you turn around correctly and check your route.

concepts.title: Describing Movement with Directions
concepts.explanation:
Compass directions become truly useful when we combine them with a distance to describe movement from one place to another. A direction on its own tells you which way to face; a distance tells you how far to go. Together they give a complete instruction.

For example, 'Walk 3 blocks North' means face the top of the map and travel three blocks that way. 'Travel 2 kilometres East' means face right and go two kilometres. We can chain several instructions together to describe a whole journey. To get from Hassan's home to the market we might say: walk 2 blocks North, then 3 blocks East.

When you follow a set of directional instructions, three things matter every time:

Follow each direction in the correct order.

Move the exact distance given in each step.

Let us follow a short journey on a grid of squares. Idris starts at a square marked X. He is told: move 2 squares North, then 3 squares East, then 1 square South, then 1 square West. If he follows each step carefully he ends up at one exact square – no other. If he muddles the order or miscounts a step, he lands somewhere else entirely. This is why counting carefully and keeping the order is so important.

Here is a helpful idea: North and South are opposites, so a step North and a step South partly cancel out. In Idris's journey he went 2 North and later 1 South, so his overall up-and-down movement is just 1 square North. He went 3 East and 1 West, so his overall left-and-right movement is 2 squares East. His whole journey is the same as a single move of 2 North and 2 East. Spotting cancelling moves is a clever shortcut you will use again with coordinates.
concepts.example: Directions also let us describe a movement we can see, not just follow one. If Zahra moves from a lower-left square to an upper-right square in one diagonal step, we say she moved North-East. If she moves from the right side of the grid to the left along the same row, she moved West. Being able to read a movement and name its direction is just as important as following instructions.

concepts.title: Understanding Coordinates
concepts.explanation:
Coordinates are a pair of numbers that describe an exact position on a grid. They are far more precise than 'near the top' or 'over on the right'. Coordinates tell us exactly how far to move across and how far to move up from a fixed starting point.

Every coordinate grid has two special lines. The x-axis is the horizontal line that runs across, from left to right. The y-axis is the vertical line that runs up and down. The point where the two axes cross is called the origin, and its coordinates are (0, 0) – zero across and zero up. Everything is measured from the origin.

A pair of coordinates is always written inside brackets with a comma between the two numbers, like this: (3, 5). The order matters enormously:

The first number is the x-coordinate. It tells you how far to move across (horizontally) from the origin.

The second number is the y-coordinate. It tells you how far to move up (vertically) from the origin.

So the coordinates (3, 5) mean: start at the origin, move 3 units right along the x-axis, then move 5 units up along the y-axis. That single point is now completely pinned down.
concepts.example: In this unit we work only in the first quadrant, which is the corner of the grid where both numbers are zero or positive. That means our points sit in the region up and to the right of the origin – the part of the grid you can see most easily. Later, in higher years, you will meet negative coordinates that reach below and to the left of the origin, but for now every coordinate you plot will be a positive number or zero.

concepts.title: Plotting and Reading Coordinates
concepts.explanation:
Plotting a point means marking it on the grid when you are given its coordinates. Follow these steps every time to plot the point (x, y):

Move x units across (to the right for a positive x).

Move y units up (upwards for a positive y).

Mark the point clearly with a small cross or dot, and label it.

For example, to plot the point (4, 2): begin at the origin, move 4 units right, then move 2 units up, and mark the spot. To plot (4, 0): move 4 units right and then 0 units up – so the point sits right on the x-axis. To plot (0, 4): move 0 units right and 4 units up – so the point sits right on the y-axis. Points with a zero always land on one of the axes, which is a good way to check your work.

Reading coordinates is the reverse skill. When a point is already marked, you work out its coordinates like this:

Find how far the point is across from the origin – that is the x-coordinate.

Find how far the point is up from the origin – that is the y-coordinate.

Write them as (x, y), across first and up second.

For example, if a point is 3 units right of the origin and 5 units up, its coordinates are (3, 5). Always trace straight down to the x-axis to read the first number, and straight across to the y-axis to read the second. Reading and plotting are two sides of the same skill, and practising both makes each one stronger.
concepts.example: It helps to notice patterns among coordinates. All points that share the same y-value – such as (1, 3), (4, 3) and (6, 3) – lie on the same horizontal line, because they are all the same height up. All points that share the same x-value – such as (4, 1), (4, 5) and (4, 6) – lie on the same vertical line, because they are all the same distance across. Spotting these patterns turns a scatter of points into an organised picture.

concepts.title: Understanding Reflections
concepts.explanation:
A reflection is a type of transformation – a way of moving a shape to a new place. When you reflect a shape, you flip it over a straight line called the mirror line (or line of reflection). The new shape you get is the mirror image of the first.

You already know what a reflection looks like. When you stand in front of a mirror, the mirror shows an image that looks just like you but flipped: if you raise your right hand, your reflection seems to raise its left. This everyday experience is exactly what happens in mathematics when we reflect a shape across a mirror line.

Reflections always obey four important properties. These are true for every reflection, no matter the shape or the mirror line:

Same size and shape. The reflected shape is exactly the same size and shape as the original. Reflection never stretches or shrinks anything, so the area and the perimeter stay the same.

Equal distances. Every point on the original and its matching point on the reflection are the same distance from the mirror line, but on opposite sides.

Perpendicular lines. If you join a point to its reflection with a straight line, that line crosses the mirror line at a right angle (90°), and the mirror line cuts it exactly in half.

Reversed orientation. The reflection is 'flipped'. If you walk clockwise around the original shape, the matching walk around the reflection goes anticlockwise. The angles stay the same, but the shape faces the other way.
concepts.example: The most important property to hold in your mind is the second one: equal distances. If a corner of a shape is 3 squares away from the mirror line, then that corner's reflection is also 3 squares from the mirror line, just on the other side. This single rule is the key to reflecting any shape accurately, as you will see next.

concepts.title: Reflecting Shapes Across a Mirror Line
concepts.explanation:
A vertical mirror line runs straight up and down, like a standing pole. A horizontal mirror line runs from side to side, like the horizon. In both cases the method for reflecting a shape is the same, and squared paper makes it much easier.

To reflect a shape across a mirror line, work one vertex (corner) at a time:

Count the number of squares from a vertex straight to the mirror line. Count along a line that meets the mirror at a right angle.

Count the same number of squares on the opposite side of the mirror line, and mark the reflected vertex there.

Repeat for every vertex of the shape.

Join the reflected vertices in the same order to complete the mirror image.

For a vertical mirror line: if a vertex is 3 squares to the left of the line, its reflection is 3 squares to the right. A point touching the line does not move at all, because its distance from the line is zero. For a horizontal mirror line the idea is identical but turned: if a vertex is 2 squares above the line, its reflection is 2 squares below it.

There is a wonderful way to check a reflection without any measuring: fold the paper along the mirror line. If your reflection is correct, the shape and its image land exactly on top of each other. This works because the two shapes are equal distances from the fold. Khadija uses this paper-folding trick to check the symmetrical henna patterns she draws before Eid.
concepts.example: Reflections can be used to build patterns. If you draw half a design against a mirror line and then reflect it, the two halves together make a symmetrical whole – the same on both sides of the line. Reflect a shape across several different mirror lines and you can create the complex repeating patterns seen in tiled floors, woven mats, and the geometric decoration of buildings.

methods.title: How to plot a point (x, y)
methods.example: Amina walks from her home to the well in the direction North-West. In which direction must she walk to come straight back home?
steps: Start at the origin (0, 0).
Move x units across to the right.
Move y units up.
Mark and label the point.

methods.title: How to reflect a shape
methods.example: Yusuf starts at a square and moves: 2 squares North, 3 squares East, 1 square South, 1 square West. Describe his overall movement in a single step.
steps: Count the squares from each vertex straight to the mirror line.
Count the same number of squares on the opposite side.
Mark each reflected vertex.
Join the vertices, then fold along the line to check.

methods.title: How to reflect a point with coordinates
methods.example: Plot the point A (5, 3) on a coordinate grid.
steps: Across a vertical line x = a: keep y, and new x = 2a − x.
Across a horizontal line y = b: keep x, and new y = 2b − y.
Check by counting the distance to the line on both sides.

methods.title: Read a point's coordinates
methods.example: A point B is 2 units to the right of the origin and 6 units up. Write its coordinates.
steps: The across-distance (x) is 2, and the up-distance (y) is 6.
Writing across first and up second gives B (2, 6).
Notice B lies higher up than it does across, because its y-value is larger than its x-value.

methods.title: Describe a movement using coordinates
methods.example: Farah starts at (2, 3). She moves 3 units right and 2 units up. What are her new coordinates?
steps: Moving right adds to the x-coordinate: 2 + 3 = 5.
Moving up adds to the y-coordinate: 3 + 2 = 5.
So her new position is (5, 5).
Moving right or up always increases the matching coordinate; moving left or down would decrease it.

methods.title: Reflect a point across a vertical line
methods.example: Reflect the point (3, 4) across the vertical mirror line x = 5.
steps: The height stays the same, so the y-coordinate is still 4.
Use new x = 2a − x with a = 5: new x = 2 × 5 − 3 = 10 − 3 = 7.
The reflection is (7, 4).
Check by counting: (3, 4) is 2 squares left of the line x = 5, and (7, 4) is 2 squares right — equal distances, so it is correct.

workedExamples.title: Name the direction and its opposite
workedExamples.prompt: Amina walks from her home to the well in the direction North-West. In which direction must she walk to come straight back home?
workedExamples.solution: Opposite directions are exact reverses. The opposite of North-West is South-East (SE). So to return home she walks South-East. A quick check: North is opposite South, and West is opposite East, so NW must be opposite SE.

workedExamples.title: Follow a movement on a grid
workedExamples.prompt: Yusuf starts at a square and moves: 2 squares North, 3 squares East, 1 square South, 1 square West. Describe his overall movement in a single step.
workedExamples.solution: Combine the opposite directions. Up and down: 2 North minus 1 South leaves 1 square North. Left and right: 3 East minus 1 West leaves 2 squares East. So his whole journey is the same as a single move of 1 square North and 2 squares East.

workedExamples.title: Plot a point
workedExamples.prompt: Plot the point A (5, 3) on a coordinate grid.
workedExamples.solution: Start at the origin (0, 0). Move 5 units right along the x-axis (across the corridor). Then move 3 units up along the y-axis (up the stairs). Mark and label the point A. Because both numbers are positive, A sits comfortably inside the first quadrant, up and to the right of the origin.

workedExamples.title: Read a point's coordinates
workedExamples.prompt: A point B is 2 units to the right of the origin and 6 units up. Write its coordinates.
workedExamples.solution: The across-distance (x) is 2, and the up-distance (y) is 6. Writing across first and up second gives B (2, 6). Notice B lies higher up than it does across, because its y-value is larger than its x-value.

workedExamples.title: Describe a movement using coordinates
workedExamples.prompt: Farah starts at (2, 3). She moves 3 units right and 2 units up. What are her new coordinates?
workedExamples.solution: Moving right adds to the x-coordinate: 2 + 3 = 5. Moving up adds to the y-coordinate: 3 + 2 = 5. So her new position is (5, 5). Moving right or up always increases the matching coordinate; moving left or down would decrease it.

workedExamples.title: Reflect a point across a vertical line
workedExamples.prompt: Reflect the point (3, 4) across the vertical mirror line x = 5.
workedExamples.solution: The height stays the same, so the y-coordinate is still 4. Use new x = 2a − x with a = 5: new x = 2 × 5 − 3 = 10 − 3 = 7. The reflection is (7, 4). Check by counting: (3, 4) is 2 squares left of the line x = 5, and (7, 4) is 2 squares right — equal distances, so it is correct.

workedExamples.title: Reflect a point across a horizontal line
workedExamples.prompt: Reflect the point (2, 6) across the horizontal mirror line y = 3.
workedExamples.solution: The across-value stays the same, so the x-coordinate is still 2. Use new y = 2b − y with b = 3: new y = 2 × 3 − 6 = 6 − 6 = 0. The reflection is (2, 0). Check by counting: (2, 6) is 3 squares above the line y = 3, and (2, 0) is 3 squares below — equal distances, so it is correct.

workedExamples.title: Properties of a reflected shape
workedExamples.prompt: Hassan reflects a rectangle across a mirror line. Its original area is 12 squares and its perimeter is 14 units. What are the area and perimeter of the reflection?
workedExamples.solution: A reflection keeps the shape exactly the same size and shape. So the reflected rectangle also has an area of 12 squares and a perimeter of 14 units. Only the orientation is reversed — the measurements never change.

workedExamples.title: Name the opposite of each direction
workedExamples.prompt: Name the opposite of each direction: a) North b) South-West c) East d) North-West.
workedExamples.solution: a) South, b) North-East, c) West, d) South-East.

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: What do all points of the form (4, n) have in common? What about all points of the form (n, 3)?
workedExamples.solution: All points (4, n) lie on a vertical line where x = 4, whatever n is. All points (n, 3) lie on a horizontal line where y = 3, whatever n is.

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: Follow the directions from square X: 2 North, 1 East, 3 South, 1 West. Describe the overall movement in one step.
workedExamples.solution: Combine opposites: 2 North and 3 South leave a net 1 South; 1 East and 1 West cancel to 0. So the overall movement is the same as a single move of 1 square South.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: Reflect each point across the vertical line x = 5: a) (3, 4) b) (7, 1) c) (0, 3).

activities.title: Make a Compass Rose
steps: Draw a large plus sign, then add diagonal lines to make an eight-armed star.
Label the four main directions: N at the top, E on the right, S at the bottom, W on the left.
Label the four in-between directions: NE, SE, SW, NW.
Stand up, face what you decide is North, and point to each direction as you name it clockwise.
Keep your compass rose – you can use it all through this unit whenever you need to check a direction.

activities.title: Coordinate Treasure Hunt
steps: Draw a grid with an x-axis and a y-axis, both numbered from 0 to 10.
Secretly mark 'treasure' at a point, such as (6, 4), and write down its coordinates.
Give a family member clues like 'go 6 across and 4 up' and let them plot the point.
Swap roles. Then try describing the route to the treasure using compass directions.

activities.title: Grid Reference Battleship
activities.materials: two matching squared grids, a pencil for each player.
steps: Each player secretly marks three small 'boats' on their own grid at chosen coordinates.
Take turns to call out a coordinate, such as (3, 5), to try to hit a boat.
Your opponent says 'hit' or 'miss'. Keep a record of the coordinates you have tried.
The first player to find all of the opponent's boats wins. This game makes reading coordinates fast and accurate.

activities.title: Fold-and-Reflect Patterns
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, scissors (with an adult's help).
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half to make a crease – this crease is your mirror line.
Draw half a shape or pattern against the fold, then cut around it while the paper is still folded.

activities.title: Direction Investigation Around Your Home
activities.materials: your compass rose from Activity 1, a notebook.
steps: Choose a fixed spot to stand, such as your front door, and decide which way is North.
Look around and record which direction each place is in: the masjid, a neighbour's house, a tree, the road.
Write instructions to walk from your door to one of these places using directions and steps.
Ask a family member to follow your instructions exactly. Did they arrive at the right place?

activities.title: Symmetry Hunt (Family Investigation)
activities.materials: your eyes, and a notebook to record what you find.
steps: Walk around your home and neighbourhood looking for reflective symmetry.
Look at leaves, patterned cloth, woven mats, doorways, and even letters of the alphabet.
For each object, imagine the mirror line and check if both sides really match.
Draw your three favourite symmetrical patterns and mark the mirror line on each.

rules.title: Coordinate Rule
rules.text: Coordinates are written (x, y): across first, then up. Along the corridor, then up the stairs. The origin is (0, 0).

rules.title: Key rule 2
rules.text: Compass Directions Clockwise from the top: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW. Opposites: N-S, E-W, NE-SW, NW-SE. Say the N or S part first (NE, not EN).

rules.title: Reflection Rule
rules.text: A reflection keeps the same size and shape – only the orientation flips. Every point and its reflection are the same distance from the mirror line, on opposite sides.

A rectangle has an area of 15 squares and a perimeter of 16 units. After reflection, what are its area and perimeter? Explain.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A reflection keeps the same size and shape, so the area is still 15 squares and the perimeter is still 16 units — only the left-right or up-down orientation changes.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A vertex of a shape is 4 squares to the left of a vertical mirror line. Where is its reflection, and how do you know?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The reflection is 4 squares to the right of the mirror line — the same distance, on the opposite side. Every point and its reflection are always the same distance from the mirror line, one on each side.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Understanding Reflections.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
A reflection is a type of transformation – a way of moving a shape to a new place. When you reflect a shape, you flip it over a straight line called the mirror line (or line of reflection). The new shape you get is the mirror image of the first.

You already know what a reflection looks like. When you stand in front of a mirror, the mirror shows an image that looks just like you but flipped: if you raise your right hand, your reflection seems to raise its left. This everyday experience is exactly what happens in mathematics when we reflect a shape across a mirror line.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Reflecting Shapes Across a Mirror Line.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A vertical mirror line runs straight up and down, like a standing pole. A horizontal mirror line runs from side to side, like the horizon. In both cases the method for reflecting a shape is the same, and squared paper makes it much easier. To reflect a shape across a mirror line, work one vertex (corner) at a time:

questions.hint: Opposite directions are exact reverses of each other.

questions.question: What are the coordinates of a point that is 4 units across and 2 units up from the origin?
questions.explanation: Coordinates are always written as (across, up), so 4 across and 2 up gives (4, 2).

questions.question: A point is plotted at (3, 7). What is its y-coordinate?
questions.hint: In (x, y), remember which number comes first.
questions.explanation: In the pair (x, y), the second number is the y-coordinate, so the y-coordinate of (3, 7) is 7.

questions.question: A point starts at (2, 5) and moves 3 units East and 1 unit South. What are its new coordinates?
questions.hint: East changes the x-coordinate; South changes the y-coordinate.
questions.explanation: Moving East increases the x-coordinate: 2 + 3 = 5. Moving South decreases the y-coordinate: 5 − 1 = 4. New position: (5, 4).

questions.question: A triangle is reflected across a vertical mirror line. Which best describes the result?
options: Same size and shape, but flipped left-to-right
Twice the size, same shape
Same size, but rotated upside down
A completely different shape
questions.answer: Same size and shape, but flipped left-to-right
questions.hint: Think about what a mirror line does to a shape's size and orientation.
questions.explanation: A reflection across a vertical mirror line keeps the shape and size exactly the same; only the left-right orientation flips.

questions.question: A shape has an area of 20 squares before being reflected. What is its area after reflection?
questions.hint: A reflection never changes the size of a shape.
questions.explanation: A reflection keeps a shape exactly the same size and shape, so its area does not change: it is still 20 squares.

questions.question: Reflect the point (2, 3) across the vertical mirror line x = 4. What are the new coordinates?
questions.hint: The y-coordinate stays the same; use new x = 2a − x.
questions.explanation: The y-coordinate stays the same at 3. New x = 2 × 4 − 2 = 6, so the reflection is (6, 3).

questions.question: A market stall is at (2, 2) on a town map. A customer walks 4 units East and 3 units North to reach the well. What are the coordinates of the well?
questions.hint: East changes x; North changes y.
